This makes the dog trigger clinically incoherent within the selected five components.

The formulation strongly links Threat → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers, but the other selected strategies (overworking, never being alone with another person) plausibly manage interpersonal threat and hypervigilance, whereas gambling does not map clearly onto the endorsed trigger/threat pattern and reads as addressing a different problem domain.

vignette: Sunita is a 66-year-old South Asian woman who has been married for nearly four decades. Her career as a midwife in a military hospital exposed her to traumatic experiences that have left lasting scars. Sunita's journey began during an incident where she was threatened by armed soldiers, leaving her feeling helpless and vulnerable. Since the trauma, Sunita frequently finds herself on edge when she perceives being watched or observed, especially when men are around or when she encounters people in uniform. These triggers have become potent reminders of her traumatic experience, immediately activating a heightened state of alertness. For instance, whenever she walks past someone in military attire, the memory of that threatening encounter surges back, causing an almost immediate and intense sense of threat. This constant vigilance has led Sunita to adopt maladaptive strategies as a way to cope with her overwhelming fear. She often throws herself into work or tasks to keep her mind occupied, finding solace in the busyness of her daily routine. In the hospital where she works, Sunita is always on guard, constantly scanning her surroundings for any sudden movements that might put her on edge again. This hypervigilance has become an ingrained habit, making it nearly impossible for her to relax even when she knows she's in a safe place. Sunita's overworking extends beyond just work-related tasks; she also ensures she is never alone with another person. This need stems from the fear that being alone might expose her to similar threats without immediate support or escape options. Her hypervigilance towards people has become so intense that even brief moments of solitude trigger panic, leading her to always seek companionship. The cycle of threat and maladaptive strategies continues to reinforce itself, creating a self-perpetuating loop. As Sunita's overworking and constant vigilance increase, she becomes more sensitive to potential triggers, making it harder for her to find any relief from her fears. For example, even a routine interaction at the hospital with male colleagues can quickly escalate into an overwhelming sense of danger, prompting her to retreat further into her maladaptive coping mechanisms. Sunita's daily life as a midwife has become increasingly challenging due to these symptoms. The constant need for companionship and her inability to relax have led to conflicts in both her professional and personal relationships. Her husband has noticed the changes but struggles to understand why she's so on edge, even at home where there are no obvious threats. Despite her efforts to manage her fears through work and vigilance, Sunita has begun to realize that these strategies are unsustainable. The relentless cycle of fear and avoidance is starting to take a toll on her mental health and well-being. It was during one particularly distressing episode at the hospital where she felt completely overwhelmed by the presence of male colleagues in uniform that she decided it was time to seek help. Sunita's primary concern now is breaking free from this cycle of fear and overworking, hoping for a future where she can feel safe and secure without constantly being on guard. She hopes therapy will provide her with new tools to manage her triggers and maladaptive behaviors, allowing her to regain control over her life and find peace in both her professional and personal spheres.
